tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper; README microbenchmark (micro/rw_experiment.c, gcc -O3) shows ext4-DAX 0.33M vs SplitFS 1.92M appends/sec (5.8x) and 4-12x lower software overhead than NOVA or ext4 DAX. Not A: the README run names no CPU model or compiler version for those numbers; experiments.md gives a Xeon E3-1225 v5 for the paper replication setup only.

corrections.hardware: README microbenchmark: Intel CPU with clflush/clflushopt, 32 GB+ DRAM, bare metal, real or emulated PM; experiments.md replication setup for the paper: Intel Xeon E3-1225 v5 @ 3.30GHz, 4 cores, 32 GB DRAM, Ubuntu 16.04
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 for the microbenchmark (README); compiler version not stated
corrections.caveats: The repository LICENSE file is Apache License 2.0 (Copyright 2019 University of Texas at Austin), but the README License section says copyright is held by UT Austin and asks commercial users to contact the authors; treat the Apache-2.0 grant as the license of record but check with the authors before commercial use. The kernel/ directory carries a patched GPL Linux 4.13 kernel (relink syscall) and the library is built on NVSL Quill. Last commit 2021-12-14. SOSP'19 paper PDF not opened (host blocked); the 5.8x and 4-12x figures are on the README page. Results were run on persistent memory (Optane or emulated), so they do not transfer to ordinary SSDs.

notes: LICENSE file is Apache-2.0, contradicting the record's proprietary license; README wording still asks for a commercial licence, so the orchestrator may prefer usability mixed. Last commit 2021-12-14 is more than 3 years old, so maintenance is abandoned.

tier_reason: VLDB'26 peer-reviewed study with a public artifact (src/, experiments/, CMakeLists.txt Release -O3 -flto -march=native, GCC 13.3.0, AMD EPYC 9654P), so it is A-eligible on methodology, but the paper with the numbers could not be opened (TU Darmstadt, arXiv and ResearchGate all blocked) and the README carries no results, so it stays at B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0, glibc 2.39, Ubuntu 24.04 (README); CMakeLists.txt Release build: -O3 -flto plus -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512bw
corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (search snippets only): zero-copy with registered buffers up to 3.5x fewer cycles per transmitted byte than default io_uring for large messages; zero-copy send/receive about 2.5x over epoll for network shuffling with large tuples; zero-copy with registered buffers about 11% higher YCSB throughput (238k tx/s); applying the guidelines to PostgreSQL's io_uring integration gave 14%
corrections.caveats: This is a study artifact (benchmark harness, a PostgreSQL patch, vmcache and fio submodules), not a reusable library; its result is guidance on configuring io_uring (registered buffers, SQPOLL, zero-copy) against epoll and default io_uring. The paper PDF is egress-blocked here (TU Darmstadt, arXiv, ResearchGate), so the numbers come from search-result snippets. The record had the 2.5x zero-copy receive figure against default io_uring; the snippet says against epoll. No license file in the repository (LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt and COPYING all 404), so the code is reference only. Two commits (2025-12-01 submission, 2026-03-31 revision). Kernels 6.15 and 6.17 built from source, with zero-copy receive bug fixes at a pinned commit.

notes: Could upgrade to A once someone opens the paper and ties the numbers to this harness; methodology (code, GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -flto -march=native, EPYC 9654P) is complete. Baseline is configuration-level (default io_uring, epoll), not a competing library.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'21 paper; the README and its linked Experiments.md artifact compare WineFS against ext4-DAX, xfs-DAX and NOVA and state an up-to-2x win on memory-mapped RocksDB and LMDB. The README has no compiler, flags or CPU model and the paper is blocked here, so it does not reach A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: outperforms ext4-DAX, NOVA and xfs-DAX by up to 2x on memory-mapped workloads (RocksDB, LMDB), and matches or beats them on Filebench and WiredTiger. Paper abstract (search snippet): in an aged setup LMDB gets 2x the write throughput of NOVA and 70% more than ext4-DAX; reads of a memory-mapped persistent radix tree have 56% lower median latency than NOVA
corrections.hardware: Experiments.md requirements: Intel Optane DC PM (500 GiB or more per socket), Cascade Lake CPU with clwb; exact CPU model not seen
corrections.workload: Memory-mapped RocksDB (YCSB) and LMDB workloads, plus Filebench and WiredTiger, on a hugepage-aware persistent-memory file system aged to 75% utilization with Geriatrix
corrections.caveats: The license is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0, which is not OSI-approved, so the code is reference only; it ships as a loadable module inside a Linux 5.1 kernel tree derived from PMFS. The SOSP'21 paper was not opened (cs.utexas.edu, pdl.cmu.edu and ACM all blocked); the paper figures come from search snippets. The record's 54% over ext4-DAX was not found; the snippet says 70% over ext4-DAX for LMDB when aged. Needs Optane PM hardware. Last commit 2022-01-13.

notes: Paper numbers come from abstract snippets only; README is qualitative (up to 2x). Last commit 2022-01-13 is more than 3 years old, so maintenance is abandoned.
